title: BM25: know it cold
summary: BM25 is word counting with three corrections: repetition stops helping, rare words count more, long documents get discounted. Worked by hand on four tiny documents, then run over the 31 lessons of this course, including one query where it picks the wrong one.
html:
Before embeddings, search was word matching. You typed words, the engine found documents containing those words, and it ranked them by some arithmetic over the counts. BM25 is that arithmetic, done carefully, and it has held up so well that it is still the baseline every new dense retriever gets measured against. Plenty of production systems still run on it alone.

Underneath it is three corrections to the obvious thing. The obvious thing is to count how many times the query's words appear in a document and rank by the total. That almost works. Here is what goes wrong and what BM25 does about it.

Correction one: repetition stops helping

A document that says "mortgage" once is probably about mortgages. A document that says it ten times is not ten times more about mortgages. The first mention tells you nearly everything, and the tenth tells you almost nothing new.

So the count gets squashed. Going from one mention to two should move the score a lot, and from nine to ten should move it hardly at all. This is called saturation.

Think of a reviewer reading your document. The first time you mention the topic, they nod. By the fourth time they have stopped being more convinced, and they are starting to wonder if you are padding.

Correction two: rare words count more

If your query is "the mortgage rate", the word "the" is in every document and tells you nothing. "Mortgage" is in a few thousand and tells you a lot. So each word gets a weight based on how rare it is across the whole collection, and common words end up nearly worthless without anyone having to keep a list of stop words.

Correction three: long documents get discounted

A forty page document mentions more words than a two paragraph one, just by being long. Without a correction, long documents win everything. So a document's score is scaled down according to how long it is compared to the average length in your collection.

All three on four tiny documents

Four documents, one query: mortgage rate. D3 is deliberately long, a single mention of mortgage buried in twenty other words.

D1  "mortgage rate dropped"                  3 words
D2  "mortgage mortgage mortgage rate"        4 words
D3  "mortgage" plus 20 other words          21 words
D4  "savings account opened"                 3 words

average length = 7.75 words

"Mortgage" appears in three of the four documents, "rate" in two, so rate is rarer and worth more. The rarity weights come out at 0.36 for mortgage and 0.69 for rate, so each occurrence of "rate" is worth about twice as much. Scoring all four:

DocumentLengthScore
D2, mortgage three times41.49
D1, each word once31.40
D3, one mention, long210.21
D4, no query words30.00

Three things to read off that table.

Saturation is doing real work. D2 says "mortgage" three times against D1's once, yet it only wins by six percent. The mortgage part of the score went from 1.33 to 1.75 when the count tripled, a rise of about a third rather than a tripling. Keyword stuffing buys almost nothing, which is exactly the intent.

Length normalisation is doing even more work. D1 and D3 both mention mortgage exactly once. D1 gets 0.48 for it and D3 gets 0.21, less than half, purely because D3 is 21 words against an average of 7.75.

Rarity sets the exchange rate. One occurrence of "rate" is worth two of "mortgage" here, and nobody configured that. It falls out of the document counts.

The formula, with every piece named

score(query, D) = sum over each query word w of:

                                  f(w,D) * (k1 + 1)
         IDF(w)  *  ---------------------------------------------
                    f(w,D) + k1 * (1 - b + b * len(D) / avg_len)

f(w,D) is how many times word w appears in document D. len(D) is the document's length in words and avg_len is the average across the collection. IDF(w) is the rarity weight, which grows as fewer documents contain w. k1 and b are the two knobs.

k1 controls how fast saturation kicks in. Higher means repetition keeps counting for longer. b controls the length discount: 0 turns it off entirely, 1 applies it in full.

Almost everyone runs k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75, including the numbers above. Those defaults came out of test collections from the 1990s and they are better described as inherited folklore than as tuned values. They are a sane starting point. If your documents are unusually uniform in length, or wildly uneven, both are worth a sweep.

What actually matters more than k1 and b

The tokeniser. BM25 matches words, so how you decide what a word is determines what can ever match. Lowercasing, splitting on punctuation, whether you stem "mortgages" down to "mortgag", whether you keep numbers, whether SKU-4417 is one token or two. In practice that choice moves results more than the knobs do, and it is the part people forget to look at when BM25 underperforms.

If you want to see it measured

Twenty five lines of Python, no library. I indexed the 31 lessons of this course as 31 documents, average length 1,137 tokens, and asked it four questions.

"how many bytes does one vector take"
   3.98  day 15, Exact kNN and why it doesn't scale        correct
"overlap between chunks"
   7.05  day 6, Chunking 101: windows, overlap, tradeoff   correct
"walk the graph to the nearest neighbour"
   7.89  day 17, HNSW I: small-world graphs                correct
"why is my search returning the wrong answer
 for a product code"
   5.51  day 22, Product quantization II                   wrong

Three out of four, with no training and no model, which is why it remains the baseline. The fourth is the honest failure and it is worth staring at. The query is about product codes, meaning identifiers. The word "product" appears constantly in the three lessons about product quantisation, so BM25 confidently returns compression material. It matched a word, not a meaning.

That failure mode is the whole argument for embeddings. Tomorrow is the mirror image: the queries where embeddings fail and BM25 is the only thing that works, which happen to be identifiers like SKU-4417.

If you remember one thing
BM25 is counting, with repetition squashed, rare words upweighted and long documents discounted. It matches words rather than meaning, and it is strong enough that beating it is the bar any retrieval change has to clear.
exercise:
One. Write your day 32 note. The clarity rating is the only lever you have on how hard these get, so use it.

Two. Take D2 from the worked example, the one with mortgage three times, and recompute its score with b set to 0, which switches length normalisation off. The length term collapses to k1 = 1.2, so the mortgage weight becomes 3 * 2.2 / (3 + 1.2) and the rate weight becomes 2.2 / (1 + 1.2). Multiply each by its rarity weight, 0.36 and 0.69, and add. Then do the same for D3, the long one, and see which document the change promotes. That tells you what b is actually buying you.
